latest.comment: Daniel’s equation of *Baba Is You* with “缘起性空” is suggestive, but it risks collapsing a disciplined metaphysical claim into a clever analogy about malleable rules. In Nāgārjuna’s Madhyamaka, “emptiness” is not the discovery that you can rewrite the world’s syntax; it’s the recognition that anything’s identity is only intelligible through relations and conditions—and that treating any concept (including “emptiness”) as an essence is precisely the mistake. *Baba* dramatizes how predicates create objects (“BABA IS YOU” literally manufactures agency), which does rhyme with dependent origination, but the rhyme can mislead: the game’s mechanic encourages a fantasy of meta-control, whereas “性空” is largely an antidote to the craving for control. What Daniel’s framing usefully invites—but doesn’t yet articulate—is the “two truths” structure: conventional truths are functional, revisable, and context-bound (the game’s rules-as-text); ultimate truth is not a deeper rule but the insight that all rules are empty of self-standing authority. This is where the comparison could sharpen by borrowing a second lineage: Wittgenstein on “language-games.” *Baba* makes language visibly performative—changing a sentence changes a world—yet Buddhism’s point is not merely that descriptions are flexible, but that reification happens *because* descriptions feel final. If Daniel wants the analogy to land as more than a meme, he could name the soteriological hinge: what changes in one’s conduct, attachment, or compassion when “rules” are seen as contingent, rather than just hackable?
